assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based accounts of technological change, skill-biased demand and the local labour-market effects of import competition changed how economists and policymakers understand wage inequality, trade and automation. The empirical designs are transparent and the results have been widely stress-tested, with replication and robustness work across countries and periods. The topic remains highly relevant given AI and automation.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Hanson and Katz are the most defensible core. Katz is the long-running anchor on skill-biased technological change and the education-technology race, Autor the central figure on tasks and the China shock, and Hanson the key co-author on trade shocks. Dorn is an important co-author but more junior. Acemoglu's earlier prize overlaps with the task framework, which complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly 1992 to the 2010s and has had decades of scrutiny, including debate over magnitudes and mechanisms. It is mature enough for recognition now.
uncertainties: Overlap with the task-based framework already recognised in the 2024 prize.
Debate over the size and persistence of the China-shock effects.
Whether the committee prefers to credit Dorn instead of Katz or Hanson.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Models of fairness and inequity aversion, together with the experimental evidence on reciprocity and costly punishment, established that non-selfish preferences are systematic and consequential for contracts, cooperation and institutions. Large-scale replication projects in experimental economics have found that lab experiments in this area hold up comparatively well. My own field is adjacent, so I weigh the replication record of the evidence and the shortage of broader field-level consequences.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is central on both the experimental and the theoretical side. Fehr and Schmidt (1999) is the canonical formal model and is rightly paired with the experimental programme. Falk is a strong contributor to field and policy applications, but the two-person pairing is the cleaner core. Bolton and Ockenfels (2000) is not on the list and is a competing model, which complicates credit.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers date from 1999-2004 and the literature is very well established. The 2002 prize recognised related behavioural work, which does not rule out further recognition of this line.
uncertainties: Credit division with Bolton and Ockenfels, who are absent from the credited names.
Judged against the breadth of impact on mainstream economics outside behavioural fields.
Whether the committee sees it as adequately recognised by earlier behavioural and experimental prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) provided a canonical mechanism for how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, and it underlies much of modern macro-finance and policy analysis after 2008. It is a foundational theoretical contribution with lasting empirical and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: The two-person core is clear because the 1997 paper is the singular origin of the credit-cycle mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator line, and Gertler's work with Bernanke was part of context already recognised in 2022. Restricting the award to Kiyotaki and Moore keeps the credit clean.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old and thoroughly absorbed into graduate teaching and policy models, so timing is not a concern.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises.
Empirical identification of the collateral channel is indirect.
Whether committee preference lies with the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm-heterogeneity trade theory shifted the unit of analysis from industries to firms. It explains selection, exporter premia and the within-industry reallocation gains from trade, and it motivated a large body of empirical work with micro-data. It is theoretically elegant and empirically productive.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the pivotal model and Helpman is a principal architect of new trade theory and heterogeneous-firm extensions, with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exports versus FDI. Redding is highly influential on quantitative and spatial extensions but later in the chain. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important co-originators on the empirical side and are missing from the credited names, which makes attribution uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The work is over twenty years old and well confirmed, and its quantitative descendants are widely used in policy analysis.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited names.
Krugman's earlier prize already recognised the new trade theory tradition.
Sensitivity of some welfare conclusions to functional-form assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi documented with granular data how household leverage and mortgage credit expansion drive booms and busts, and how debt overhang depresses demand. This reshaped the post-2008 understanding of the macroeconomy, and the identification relies on cross-sectional variation that has been examined extensively. The work has direct consequences for macroprudential and household-debt policy.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear joint originators of the household-debt view of the Great Recession and of the credit-supply research programme. Campbell is a major finance economist, but his contribution to household finance and asset pricing is a different literature, so the credit line fits poorly with this discovery.
assessment.maturity: The central papers appeared from about 2009 to 2015 and have been broadly replicated and extended internationally. Recognition is plausible but the work is somewhat more recent than other candidates.
uncertainties: Debate over the causal weight of credit supply versus other factors.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on financial crises.
The relatively recent timing may argue for waiting.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run top-income series built from tax records transformed the empirical study of inequality and shaped the global policy debate. The data infrastructure (the World Inequality Database) is a public good. Methodological debate on measurement, such as survey versus tax data and treatment of capital income and retirement wealth, warrants caution, and the strength of the causal and theoretical contribution is more limited than the descriptive impact.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the original authors of the top-incomes series, and Zucman extended the work to offshore and wealth data. Credit is complicated by the long tradition of Kuznets, Atkinson and others. Atkinson, who is deceased, and other inequality scholars are not available for credit.
assessment.maturity: The work is more than twenty years old and its measurement claims have been debated at length. Publication of the data and methods makes the evidence unusually checkable.
uncertainties: Open dispute over some measurement choices and wealth-concentration estimates.
Weight given to descriptive and data contributions relative to causal or theoretical ones.
Policy-prescriptive and political dimensions of the work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Careful empirical work on adverse selection and moral hazard in insurance markets, combining theory, quasi-experimental and experimental designs such as the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, produced credible evidence on the welfare costs of selection. Randomised and well-powered designs are strong on credibility. The theory-meets-data approach has influenced health policy and public finance.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav are the leading joint figures in the empirical analysis of selection markets, and Finkelstein led the Oregon experiment with others. Salanie is a prominent theorist and empiricist of insurance, but the empirical-welfare programme centres on the first two. Chiappori and Salanie's positive-correlation test is a key precursor.
assessment.maturity: The central work spans about 2004 to 2020 and is highly regarded, but the field is relatively young for the prize. It may need further time and long-run assessment.
uncertainties: Relative recency compared with long-established candidates.
Credit shared with other health-policy experimenters, such as the Oregon team.
Generalisability of context-specific findings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linking population administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility across places and groups created a new empirical research agenda with large policy relevance. The transparent, large-sample designs and open data releases are strong on credibility and checkability, although some neighbourhood-effect and causal estimates depend on identifying assumptions that remain under debate.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader of the programme. Hendren is the main co-author on causal place effects and the Opportunity Atlas. Friedman and Katz are major collaborators, with Katz also appearing in other candidates, so the set of laureates is ambiguous.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from about 2014 to 2022, so the longer-run confirmation and replication record is still developing. Chetty's other work, such as the optimal-taxation research listed in B044, is a separate matter for this ranking.
uncertainties: Relatively recent timing and ongoing methodological debate on causal neighbourhood effects.
Credit division among a large collaborative team.
Possible preference for a broader Chetty-centred award across several lines.
